https://macworld.com/article/3268030/the.html:
Macworld

Apple unveiled the first iPod on October 23, 2001, exactly a quarter-century ago. Our original reviewer said the device looked great, had a screen that was easy to read, featured navigation that was “the best I’ve ever seen,” and was “definitely” worth $399. But how well has it stood the test of time? Would anyone buy a first-gen iPod today?

As a keepsake, a cool bit of vintage memorabilia? Absolutely, and at astonishingly high prices. But as a workhorse portable music player for everyday use? Not so much. Technology has progressed quite a long way in the past 25 years.

To demonstrate this, here are a few interesting facts and figures to show how the iPod compares to the iPhone Duo, Apple’s latest handheld device (and music player, among other things). See if you’d be willing to make the tech-spec sacrifices necessary in order to enjoy this piece of history.

Processing power

The original iPod’s PortalPlayer PP5002 chip ran two 90MHz cores. Totally acceptable for 2001.

The iPhone Duo, on the other hand, isn’t even Apple’s most powerful current mobile device. Early reviews suggest the iPhone 18 Pro runs both a little quicker and a little cooler, but with a maximum CPU clock rate of 4.93GHz, its six-core A20 Pro chip is roughly 50 times as fast.

The Duo also has 12GB of RAM, a mere 375 times as much as the iPod’s 32MB. It probably has a bit more processing muscle, on balance.

Storage

This is always a brutal comparison because storage hardware has plummeted in price over the years, while storage needs have skyrocketed. But here we go.

The original iPod offered a maximum capacity of 10GB, enough (according to Apple’s marketing materials) to hold 2,000 songs. The iPhone Duo tops out at 2TB. That’s 200 times as much.

Foundry

Camera

The iPhone Duo has actually come in for some mild criticism over its camera setup, which doesn’t include a telephoto lens. But it still boasts four separate lenses for various situations: 48MP wide and ultrawide as your main shooting option on the rear, 12MP on the cover, and a neat 4MP camera hidden beneath the display for FaceTime.

The original iPod didn’t have any cameras at all. iPods wouldn’t get a still camera for another nine years, on the 4th-gen iPod touch. It had two of these, rated at 0.7MP and 0.3MP.

Screen

This could be painful.

The original iPod’s display measured just 2 inches corner to corner, with a resolution of 160 x 128. (It was monochrome, of course.) The Duo has two full-color screens, inside and out; even the smaller of the two is vastly bigger and sharper, at 5.4 inches and 1398 x 2034 pixels. The outer display is 7.6 inches and 1878 x 2670: the same number of pixels as 245 iPod screens. But it does have a slight crease, so there’s that.

Apple

Water/dust resistance

It was considered unwise to drop the original iPod in the bath. The device didn’t have an IP rating and was not water-resistant.

The iPhone Duo, by contrast, has an IP rating of IP68, pretty much the highest rating you’ll see on a consumer tech product. That signifies that the device is dust-tight and capable of handling immersion in more than 1m of water.

Dimensions & weight

The original iPod measured roughly 102 x 62 x 19.8mm. It weighed 184g. (That’s 4 x 2.4 x 0.8 inches and 6.5oz, if you prefer imperial.)

The Duo’s dimensions are a little more complicated because they depend on whether it’s folded or unfolded. In its more compact form, it measures 118 x 84 x 11.3 mm, so a little longer, a little wider, and close to half the thickness. And when unfolded, those differences become even more exaggerated: at 117.8 x 165 x 5.2 mm it offers far more real estate, most of which is screen, while being a quarter the thickness.

The Duo’s weight is always the same: 254g, or 9oz. It’s a fair bit heavier than the iPod.

Price

The iPod started at $399 when it launched in 2001. That’s about $750 in 2026 money. But the Duo is way more expensive than even the inflation-adjusted figure, starting at an eye-watering $1,999.

25 years of progress

For the price of a single iPhone Duo you could get a couple of original iPods (even adjusted for 25 years of inflation) and still have enough left to buy an Apple Watch or two. But there’s a reason why the Duo costs so much more.

It has 200 times as much storage, 375 times as much RAM, 245 times as many pixels on just one of its screens, and the ability to perform a million times as many functions… including taking photos. And folding.

But will the iPhone Duo become a cultural phenomenon, upending multiple industries and finding a place in millions of lives (not to mention numerous art galleries)? Only time will tell. Let’s revisit this discussion in another 25 years.

Ever since the 10th-gen iPad’s 2022 redesign to match the rest of the lineup, the iPad lineup has been pretty clear. There’s the iPad Pro, which has the latest features and the best performance, the iPad Air in the middle, the smaller iPad mini, and the entry-level model with an older A-series chip and display. As such, we’ve always recommended the iPad Air for most people looking for an iPad with a smart combination of price and specs. However, after the recent hikes added $150 to the price, the Air is a lot less attractive than it was for $599, especially since it hasn’t gotten a meaningful upgrade in years.

The upcoming iPad mini—expected to launch as part of Apple’s “Pro and Tell” event next week—is shaping up to become the new balanced mid-ranger. While it won’t offer an M-series processor or a screen as larger as even the smaller iPad Air, the overall package is rumored to be significantly more advanced and feature-rich than the Air offers. In fact, once the new iPad mini launches, I see little reason why the Air even needs to exist.

Au revoir, LED

Disregarding the size, the iPad Air and iPad mini offer comparable Liquid Retina (LED) screens. With both models, you get the same maximum brightness, wide color P3 gamut, True Tone support, Apple Pencil compatibility, antireflective coating, etc. The iPad mini does come with a slightly higher pixel density of 326 ppi (compared to the Air’s 264 ppi) due to its smaller size, but that’s about it.

The M4 iPad Pro was the first Apple tablet to adopt an OLED panel, unlocking true blacks and crisper colors. After two years of exclusivity, OLED is finally rumored to expand to another iPad. Based on Apple’s pattern, one would assume that would be the iPad Air, but somewhat surprisingly, it’s reportedly coming to the mini first.

Earlier this year, Apple introduced its Creator Studio subscription service. For a reasonable monthly or annual fee, Creator Studio bundles some of Apple’s most popular productivity apps, including Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, and Photomator, into a fully connected suite, and unlocks exclusive AI-centric perks in the free iWork suite, allowing users to choose from premium templates and generate photos in Pages, Numbers, and Keynote.

However, compared to the Gemini integration in Google Workspace, the AI offerings in Creator Studio are somewhat lackluster. That, however, is seemingly about to change. According to a Pages update that was briefly published to the App Store, Apple is about to expand the AI toolbox in iWork, providing subscribers with a Google Workspace-like experience.

Meet Intelligent Assistant

As stated in the release notes of a now-pulled Apple Pages update, Creator Studio apps will soon adopt a Gemini-like tool called Intelligent Assistant. Per the change log, the beta feature requires iOS 27 and will allow Creator Studio users to:

  • Start a first draft, then edit, organize, and elevate your writing with an assistant that understands your document;
  • Get guidance on where to start, learn how to use advanced features, or try a suggestion to see what’s possible;
  • Draft a section, adjust your tone, or generate images and shapes using natural language
  • Search for up-to-date information on a topic and incorporate it into your document.

Foundry

Based on the official description, it appears that Intelligent Assistant will significantly elevate the existing Writing Tools with deeper document context awareness, help research topics using fresh information, and more. While users can already achieve similar results using Siri AI on iOS 27, it seems Intelligent Assistant will be more deeply integrated into Pages, Numbers, and Keynote, providing a more intuitive ideation, creation, and editing flow.

Other Creator Studio perks included with the removed update include “a new collection of professionally-designed templates,” along with curated videos in the Content Hub “that add motion and depth to your document.”

Where’s the update?

I was able to download Pages version 15.4.1 right after Apple published it and before its swift removal. However, despite having an active Creator Studio subscription, I was unable to locate or use the all-new Intelligent Assistant. Even stranger, at the time of writing, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote were completely unavailable to download from the U.S. App Store—presumably as Apple resolved the matter.

Later in the day, Apple pushed version 15.4.2, which includes bug fixes and adds iPhone Duo support, skipping 15.4.1 entirely. However, I’ve been unable to activate or use the Intelligent Assistant feature. It’s also strange that Apple wouldn’t have announced the feature with a press release or some other fanfare.

So Apple either accidentally posted a change log meant for a future update or is rolling out the feature gradually to users. Whether we see Intelligent Assistant in the coming days or it’s delayed for a few weeks, one thing is clear: Apple is finally aiming to take Creator Studio to the next level for AI power users.

With an iconic look, smart design, and massive commercial success, the AirPods are one of the finest Apple products to launch in the Tim Cook era. And unlike some Apple hardware I could mention, these neat wireless earbuds just keep getting better and better, making worthwhile steps forward in the 2nd- (wireless charging), 3rd- (improved design and sound quality), and 4th- (ANC) generation models. What’s Apple got in store for the AirPods 5? Plenty.

Launched alongside the iPhone Duo and Apple Watch Series 12, this year’s AirPods have five main attractions, running the gamut from improved ANC (active noise cancellation) on both models to a truly unexpected price cut. All signs point to another home run.

But do the AirPods 5 live up to the hype? I spent three weeks testing them thoroughly to find out. From battery performance to sound quality, my in-depth review has everything you need to decide if these are the earbuds for you. Should you upgrade from a set of AirPods 3 or 4? Are these a better choice than the AirPods Pro 3? How do they compare to earbuds from rival companies? Don’t worry, I’m here to help.

For broader advice, check out our guides to the best AirPods and the best wireless earbuds.

David Price / Foundry

AirPods 5: Design and fit

The AirPods 5 have the same external design as the previous generation, and largely the same design as every AirPods model going back to 2016: the stems have got shorter over the years, but the classic shape and shiny white finish remain instantly recognizable. They look great, in short, but don’t expect anything radically new.

But there are a couple of minor changes to the design which are worth mentioning. One is that the new earbuds (and their case) are rated as significantly more water-resistant than the previous model, with the IP rating bumped from IP54 to IP57. The second number refers to liquid ingress, and in this case indicates that whereas the AirPods 4 were protected against jets of water, the AirPods 5 can handle immersion up to 1m for 30 minutes… although I wouldn’t recommend testing this out. More of a peace-of-mind type of upgrade.

A change you’re more likely to notice if you opt to spend an extra $20 on the model with the wireless charging case is the addition of a volume swipe function to the force sensor on both stems: swipe up to increase the volume, swipe down to decrease it. It’s odd that this feature isn’t available on the cheapest AirPods 5, but neither AirPods 4 model got it, and in principle this is a handy addition to your controls. An unexpectedly loud track starts playing on shuffle? No need to dig out your iPhone, you can simply lower the volume with a swipe. The only issue is that it’s a little awkward to use because the AirPods 5 fit quite loosely; trying to swipe the control sometimes just makes the earbuds move in the ear. The AirPods Pro, by comparison, have a firmer fit which makes it easier to use their swipe control.

David Price / Foundry

So let’s talk fit. Unlike the AirPods Pro, which come with detachable eartips in a range of sizes and can be further customised by using aftermarket foam tips, the AirPods 5 continue to use an integrated earbud in the same material as the rest of the device. That means you’re stuck with a single, standard shape and size. If it doesn’t fit, you’re out of luck.

That might sound unappealing, and it’s true that the range of interchangeable eartips means that (once you’ve put in the work experimenting with different sizes and potentially shopping around for third-party alternatives) the AirPods Pro will deliver a better fit and superior passive sound isolation. But in my experience the standard AirPods generally offer a good, secure, and comfortable fit. My AirPods 5 move around a little more than my AirPods Pro 3, hence the issues with the swipe control, but this very rarely causes any other problems.

I was skeptical when the time came to do an exercise test. As I’ve written elsewhere, I rarely feel comfortable wearing earbuds during exercise unless they have ear hooks, fins, or a neck band, but the AirPods 5 held up surprisingly well. Once I broke a sweat, they started to feel slippery and precarious, and a few specific activities–kneeling dumbbell rows, getting off the stationary bike–did make them fall out. Most of the time, however, they stayed in… including, triumphantly, the full duration of a 40-minute treadmill session.

I’d still prefer to have one pair of headphones for general listening, and another specialised set (more secure in the ear, perhaps more bass-focused, but above all cheaper) for sports. But in a pinch, and preferably indoors rather than in an environment with gutters and puddles, these can fill in reasonably effectively as exercise buds.

While we’re on the subject of eartips vs. integrated earbuds, bear in mind that the latter approach is better in other ways. Integrated earbuds don’t penetrate so far into the ear canal; some people don’t like the feel of silicone eartips and find them oddly intrusive, whereas you hardly know the AirPods 5 are there. This design also takes up less room in the case, which means the AirPods 5 case is smaller and noticeably more comfortable in the pocket than that of the AirPods Pro 3. There are no worries about an eartip detaching and getting lost. And the AirPods 5 are both easier to clean and (this is disgusting, but there’s no other way to say it) less prone to collecting earwax than versions with a detachable eartip.

David Price / Foundry

So for me these get two thumbs up for both fit and design. But ear canals vary, and the one-size-fits-all nature of the AirPods 5 makes it essential that you either try before you buy, or ensure that you can return them afterwards if you find that the shape is not suitable for you.

AirPods 5: Sound quality

As with the fit, I was pleasantly surprised by the sound quality delivered by the AirPods 5 while being conscious that the Pro model does sound noticeably better.

I spent a while obsessively playing the same Pink Floyd track (“The Great Gig in the Sky”) alternating between the AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 to spot the differences. After close comparison, these were obvious: there’s a deeper, richer, and more immersive sound on the AirPods Pro, and the bass hits harder and more bodily when the vocals come in. But that doesn’t mean the AirPods 5 are bad. On the contrary, they delivered a warm, clear sound with plenty of detail and the ability to hit higher volumes without any distortion. And on my first play, before I’d given the Pros a go, I thought they were pretty great. Comparison is the thief of joy, as they say.

Keen to explore the disparity in bass performance, I next turned to some pulsing disco (“Supernature” by Cerrone) for a proper test. The AirPods 5 did manage to deliver decent bass once I cranked up the volume. But it just doesn’t compare to the AirPods Pro 3. What I was missing was that kinetic, almost hostile bass kick that you feel in the back of the head. (That’s about all you can expect from even a good pair of in-ears. The visceral body blow is the domain of high-end over-ears.) When I went back to the AirPods 5 for a second attempt, they felt polite by comparison. The AirPods 5 did fine, but if you love dance, disco, or anything that depends on heavy bass, an upgrade to the Pro model will be worth the money.

Away from the most bass-dependent musical genres, the AirPods 5 consistently delivered beautifully warm, clear, and faithful audio. A baroque piano piece was handled with sensitivity to the texture and atmosphere of the recording; the fine details and discernible muttering put me in the room with the musician. A 1950s jazz track was rich and smoky and exhilarating. And when I fancied a bit of art-pop, I could hear the crackling fire at the start of “Horse And I” by Bat for Lashes just as easily as its soaring multilayered vocals.

I really like the sound quality of the AirPods 5. It’s not as good as that of the AirPods Pro 3, particularly on bass-heavy tracks, but let’s remember that the Pro models cost $249, whereas these start at $129. For a set of affordable in-ears without the benefit of detachable eartips, these are fantastic.

David Price / Foundry

AirPods 5: Active noise cancelation

While we’re talking audio, it’s worth discussing active noise cancellation (ANC). For the uninitiated, this feature involves the headphones monitoring ambient audio and then playing the opposite sound wave directly into your ear, cancelling it out. (Passive noise isolation, by contrast, simply involves a snug-fitting earbud blocking out unwanted sounds.) It’s a clever and often very effective way to escape background conversation, traffic sounds, commuter hustle and bustle, and so on.

ANC is key to the AirPods 5 for two reasons. First, Apple claims to have improved this feature significantly from the AirPods 4 (specifically, that this product delivers “up to 1.5x more,” however that’s measured). And second, the feature is now available on both versions of the AirPods 5, whereas the AirPods 4 were split into ANC and non-ANC tiers.

Getting ANC at all for $129 is very nice indeed. But even with the “1.5x” improvement, I have to say that it’s not the best example of the tech I’ve ever tested. I put on some YouTube videos while wearing the AirPods 5 (with nothing playing, just the ANC doing its thing) and was still able to keep up with what was being said fairly easily. It was just muted. When I repeated the test with the AirPods Pro 3, the conversations became very difficult to follow, which is exactly what I’m looking for while commuting.

I had similar results when using the AirPods 5 to keep down the volume of visiting children in the next room: I could still hear their laughing and clapping all too clearly. And while the background hubbub on a train was dampened fairly well, spoken announcements came through clearly. You might think that’s a good thing, but there’s a specific mode (adaptive audio, which I found very effective) designed to allow through some sounds but filter out others, and when I’ve got ANC on, I’d prefer to eliminate almost everything.

Of course, much of the time you’ll be combining ANC with audio of some kind: music, a podcast, an audiobook. The combination of the two should drastically reduce the distraction and annoyance of inconsiderate fellow passengers. But I’m quite fond of silence, and the AirPods 5 alone may struggle to achieve this.

David Price / Foundry

AirPods 5: Siri AI and other features

Aside from ANC, Apple is keen to talk up the AirPods 5 for their AI features. My experiences with this were rather mixed.

To start with, I used the Live Translation feature to navigate a conversation in French (specifically a “real French conversation” I found on YouTube, with all the messiness and grammatical irregularity one would expect in real life), and the results were incomprehensible. When I switched to one labelled “super easy,” the AI managed much better, but there were still torturous pauses after each phrase. This may be an impressive proof of concept and a glimpse of a multilingual future, but for now it doesn’t strike me as useful.

Note that Live Translation is not a new feature; it was announced in September last year and is also available on the AirPods 4 with ANC. But Apple again hyped it up in the press release for this product, so I thought it was important to give it a try.

The AirPods 5 are also compatible with Siri AI, the improved version of Apple’s Siri voice assistant. But again, this isn’t a latest-gen exclusive; the AirPods 4 with ANC and the last two generations of AirPods Pro have the same feature. And while I was impressed with Siri AI’s accuracy and feature set–I asked about an upcoming social engagement using rather careless natural language, for example, and it tracked down the correct details in my calendar–the responses were a little slow, to the extent that I wasn’t always sure if the system had heard me.

There are also some concerns with device overlap. For one thing, I’m not convinced that I need my headphones to have Siri AI, when my iPhone, iPad, and MacBook all have it already. There are situations when it makes sense and is more convenient to access Siri AI via the AirPods, but quite a few of those involve me looking like I’m talking to myself. That impression can be lessened, admittedly, by the ability to respond to Siri AI by nodding or shaking your head, but the initial query still needs to be spoken out loud.

On one occasion I said, “Hey Siri” to ask a question, my HomePod (which has Siri but not Siri AI) responded that it couldn’t answer that, and then the AirPods kicked in and took charge, seemingly unaware another device had already taken a swing. It just doesn’t feel like a completely seamless system at this stage.

David Price / Foundry

AirPods 5: Battery and charging

For the AirPods I tested (the ones which come with a wireless charging case), Apple estimates a battery life of up to five hours with ANC enabled. That’s an improvement on the previous generation, whose equivalent model was capable of just 4 hours with ANC. If you’re prepared to do without ANC, you should be able to squeeze out an extra two hours per charge.

In testing, those numbers proved accurate, if you keep the words “up to” in mind: my test unit died after 4 hours and 43 minutes of continuous music playback at medium volume with ANC enabled. Technically, they soldiered on with one surviving earbud for another 10 minutes, but that won’t do you much good.

The real convenience and joy of AirPods, of course, is the fact that putting them away in their slim case charges them from its larger battery. Apple estimates that, if you start with fully charged earbuds and a fully charged case, you’ll be able to get around 22 hours of total playback. I think that’s fair. Based on my tests, the case is capable of roughly four full charges, which means five complete rundowns (and somewhere between 22 and 25 hours of playback) before you need to plug it in.

David Price / Foundry

Charging in the case is conveniently speedy, particularly at low levels. Apple boasts that just five minutes of charging will give you around an hour of playback, and while my testing suggested this is slightly optimistic (my AirPods 5 lasted for 51 minutes after their micro-charge), it’s still impressive. A full charge from 0 to 100 percent took me 103 minutes, but a big chunk of that time is spent mopping up the last few percentage points; just half an hour in the case got me to 75 percent.

While the non-linear charging speeds might seem strange to those of us who aren’t battery scientists, it’s really the best way for things to work out. When speed isn’t an issue, you can just pop the AirPods in their case and leave them overnight, and get the value of a full charge the next day. But in an audio emergency, when for example you’ve been hammering album after album on an international flight, and they just can’t take it any more, a short break will be enough for several more hours of playback.

By now you’ve seen the keynote, watched the ads, and read the early reviews. You know what the iPhone Duo’s features are. But what is it like to use it, right here at the launch?

We’re working on our iPhone Duo review, but as the Apple Stores open up today to hand over a precious few preorders and disappoint legions of would-be drop-in buyers, I wanted to share some initial impressions. Here are six things I discovered on my first day with the iPhone Duo.

Outside bad, inside great

When you have the fold folded, it’s not a great experience. Even with the home row and controls on the side, it’s the smallest iPhone display in many years, and most apps just aren’t formatted for the odd shape. Unless you’ve been clinging to your iPhone 13 mini all this time, you’re likely to find that even optimized apps, which put their controls off on the right edge to allow more vertical room, are frustratingly small.

If you are an iPhone mini diehard, the screen won’t bother you, but the massively fat and chunky form factor will. What good is a small screen when the phone is so thick and wide that it’s definitely not going to fit in the pocket of a pair of tight jeans?

The actual display quality is fine, and so is the outside selfie camera. But that outside screen is for quick-hit info checking, firing off a short reply, dialing a phone number, or asking Siri stuff. That said, there is one huge benefit: the keyboard. While it takes up like half the vertical space, the extra-wide shape makes the whole keyboard a lot larger and easier to use. It’s even wider than an iPhone 18 Pro Max keyboard, and the extra few millimeters really help.

However, the inside display is a delight and makes me want this same nanotexture treatment on all iPhones. It has a lovely paper-like feel to the touch and seriously cuts down on glare, while still remaining bright and sharp. Granted, blacks aren’t as deep as on a glossy screen, but it’s still very good, and the trade-off is totally worth it for all the glare (and crease) you don’t have to deal with.

When using the inner display, the Duo feels super thin and light, comfortable and easy to use. The more time you spend with the Duo unfolded, the more you love it.

A status bar and Dynamic Island upgrade

Without a camera cutout in the middle of the display (inside or out), Apple moved the Dynamic Island to the upper right corner. It surrounds the front camera when closed, and just pops up out of nowhere on the inner display.

It’s actually in a really great spot, expanding down vertically as necessary. I prefer it to the centered one, and it makes me want Apple to stuff the camera up in the corner on all future iPhones.

There’s a new status bar element beneath it that, again, is a step up from current iPhones. A bar at the top shows battery (with percentage if you like), the Wi-Fi symbol in the middle is your Wi-Fi strength, and a series of four dots underneath is your cellular strength. It’s a brilliant little mash-up that again, should make its way to other iPhones.

Foundry

No information is lost, space is saved, and it takes all of two seconds to get used to the change. Plus, you can tap on it to show the entire Control Center (so you don’t have to do an awkward edge swipe), which is already my favorite thing. When you do, the symbols separate and expand to show more detail.

StandBy any time

Another trick the Duo can do that other iPhones can’t is enter Standby mode when not connected to power. Just lock the screen and then stick it in “tent” posture, and it becomes a nice little smart clock for your desk. Or open it partially like a book, and you get a two-page Standby mode view.

It’s clever, it’s fun, and it makes the “put my iPhone down on the desk while working” thing actually useful. I can see this being the preferred way for Duo owners to place their phone when out with friends—keeping their phone out of their hands while still letting them see the clock or showing a conversation-starting photo album.

Dear Apple, please give every iPhone with an always-on display the option to go into Standby mode when not connected to power. Even lying flat on a desk, it would be nice.

Foundry

The cameras are (mostly) fine

The 48MP main camera is not as good as that on the iPhone 18 Pro, even if you ignore the aperture blades. It starts to get a little noticeable in low light. But it’s close, and it’s certainly good enough. The ultra-wide is as good as Apple’s best, and as useful as ever for macro shots.

Weirdly, you get like half the Pro camera controls from the iPhone 18 Pro. There’s no aperture control (of course), no histogram, no shutter speed. But you do get white balance, manual focus with focus peaking, and the new photographic styles with adjustable skin texture and grain.

The front-facing selfie camera has the center stage functions (auto-rotate and auto-zoom) introduced in the iPhone 17 line with the new 18-megapixel sensor, but this isn’t that sensor. It’s the older 12MP sensor, and the dynamic range and clarity just aren’t as good. It’s fine, but the newer 18MP sensor on the other recent iPhones is better.

But that inside selfie camera. Oh. Oh no. No, that’s a potato. It takes blurry, awful 4MP photos that have a bunch of post-processing to over-sharpen and restore some detail. It’s kind of good enough for a FaceTime call in good lighting, but it’s absolute trash compared to the selfie cam since iPhone X. If this is the cost of an under-display camera, I don’t want it.

Here’s a neat trick, though: When you’re in selfie mode, you can flip the whole Duo around, and there’s a “Slide to show camera” bar that flips the interface to the outside screen while turning off the inside screen so you don’t accidentally interact with it. Then you can take a selfie with the 48MP main camera. It’s pretty awesome, really.

The apps matter most

There are three classes of iPhone Duo apps, and you’ll discover all of them while learning how crucial they are in the first five minutes of using your iPhone Duo.

Old garbage apps: These are apps that haven’t been updated for the dynamic sizing of iOS 27. They have a black bar on the side of the outside screen and appear centered against a black background on the inside screen (though you can swipe to move it from the center to either side). These apps suck on the Duo. They put their interface buttons on the bottom, which makes them feel even smaller, and they waste all that space.

A lot of old apps, small apps from small companies (like a local bank chain), and apps with notoriously bad UI design, such as most car apps or insurance apps. It’s just a terrible experience, and there are a lot of these that probably won’t ever be updated. Thankfully, you can force these apps into split view with a Duo-optimized app that’ll make the awful experience slightly better.

iOS 27 apps: Apps that updated to use iOS 27’s resizable and reconfigurable layout fare a lot better. When you use them on the inside screen, they fill the width and often give you a sidebar, or split info between an index and content. The Tesla app just updated to use this, as does Microsoft Outlook and Robinhood, among others. It’s something of a stopgap, but is a signal that the developer is working on a proper Duo app. In fact, Robinhood says a Duo-optimized app will be available on launch day.

You still get interface elements that don’t use the left/right sidebars, and they don’t understand all the “poses” for Duo, but at least you can go from iPhone app outside to iPad app inside, essentially, and it’s really nice.

Duo-optimized apps: Oh, these are fun. When an app uses the Duo-specific developer frameworks, it will put the interface elements out of the way on the side, mitigating the tiny outside screen (somewhat). Inside, it will fill the display, morph to make correct use of portrait and landscape view, and many times, move stuff away from the crease when you slightly fold the Duo into “book” form.

This is how the Duo is meant to be used, and it’s really great when it’s there. Most of Apple’s apps work like this, as you would expect, but some don’t (I’m looking at you, Wallet and Apple Store). Third-party apps that have updated to Duo-optimized apps all feel great. MLB, Spotify, Slack, Yelp, Instagram, TikTok, Things, Fantastical, Carrot Weather…there are plenty of popular apps with full Duo support, and the experience when you use them is awesome.

But just as many important apps don’t work well on Duo at all. Given the book-sized open position and glare-free, paper-like coating on the display, you would think ebook readers would prioritize Duo support. But Kindle is flat-out busted, and glitches out when you try to show the menu in reader mode. (I actually had to close the Duo and return the app to the outside screen just to get out of the page view!) The Libby app is in desperate need of an update, too.

The app situation is currently all over the place. Gmail supports the iOS 27 reactive sizing, but has a poor layout for widescreen. Google News is an old-style iPhone app that looks and feels terrible on the big screen. Video apps like Netflix, Paramount+, and Prime Video have nice Duo optimizations, but Hulu and Disney+ do not. Lyft, yes. Uber, no.

It’s the Wild West right now, and the situation changes daily. The number of apps you use that are Duo-optimized (or at least iOS 27 optimized) is a crucial part of how much you’ll like using this phone, and it’s a quickly moving target.

I miss Face ID already

You’ve seen a lot of early reviewers complain about the lack of Face ID. They are correct.

We get emails all the time from people who miss Touch ID and want it back. I guess they forget what it was like to unlock their iPhone with gloves, or wet/dirty hands, or to have to reach to a certain spot, or to have their lock screen notifications jump away because you accidentally opened your phone when you unlocked it.

All those experiences come right back with the iPhone Duo. Except one—Apple added a delay on the lock screen. When you put your finger on the side button at the lock screen, your phone unlocks so you can see your notifications, but it doesn’t open yet. A little message shows a fingerprint icon and “Rest to Open” at the top of the display, and your iPhone opens to the home screen after a short pause with your finger on the button.

Foundry

In the first hour with the Duo alone, there were dozens of situations in which I wanted to fill in a password, download an app, or make a purchase that required me to authenticate with Touch ID. And every single time, I was reminded that I now had to do something where Face ID would simply automatically authenticate. I registered both thumbs and my index finger with Touch ID, and that certainly helps, but it’s still slower and more awkward than Face ID.

It has a lovely paper-like feel to the touch and seriously cuts down on glare, while still remaining bright and sharp. The apps matter most

Old garbage apps: These are apps that haven’t been updated for the dynamic sizing of iOS 27. Apple’s first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, officially goes on sale today, Friday, October 23, but getting hold of one could prove difficult. Preorders opened on October 16 and delivery estimates slipped rapidly, with Macworld’s U.S. tracking showing waits stretching to January 25, 2027 within around half an hour. Apple is still accepting orders, but there is another option for buyers who don’t want to wait: Apple has confirmed that limited numbers of the iPhone Duo will be available for walk-in customers at Apple Stores in the U.S., U.K. and other selected markets on launch day. Supplies are expected to be extremely limited, however, and there’s no guarantee of getting one without a preorder. Prices start at $1,999/£1,999.

The Duo opens like a book from a compact 5.4-inch phone into a much larger 7.6-inch device. Apple describes the internal screen as its largest-ever iPhone display, with 50 percent more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, while the outer display provides more than 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest difference is obviously the folding design, but Apple has done more than simply add a hinge. The iPhone Duo ships with iOS 27.1, which adapts to different positions and orientations with fold-specific interface and multitasking features. These include Split View, hands-free FaceTime and video, StandBy without charging, and layouts that move seamlessly between the two screens. Apple Pencil USB-C support is also coming later in 2026.

The other major changes are the 7.6-inch nano-texture inner display, Touch ID replacing Face ID, an A20 Pro processor with vapor-chamber cooling, and a dual-battery system designed around the two halves of the phone. Apple has also introduced camera features that exploit the second screen, including Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and Duo FaceTime.

Much of the pre-launch reporting proved accurate: the Duo name, book-style design, roughly 7.7- and 5.4-inch screens, Touch ID, two 48MP rear cameras, two front-facing cameras, A20 Pro, C2 modem, MagSafe and the white/dark-blue colors were all anticipated.

iPhone Duo at a glance

  • Apple’s first folding iPhone, with 5.4-inch outer and 7.6-inch inner displays.
  • Touch ID replaces Face ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button.
  • A20 Pro with vapor-chamber cooling, including a new 2nm manufacturing process.
  • Dual-battery architecture, giving up to 44 hours of video playback on the outer display.
  • Fold-specific iOS and camera features, including Split View, Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and hands-free use.

iPhone Duo: Top 10 features

iPhone Duo release date: When did it launch?

Apple announced the iPhone Duo on September 9, 2026, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Sales began on October 23, following preorders on October 16.

The October 23 launch covers more than 70 countries and regions, including the U.S. and U.K., with another 28 markets following on October 30. The Duo will also be available through Apple Stores, selected carriers and authorized retailers, although availability varies by market.

As of October 23, Apple was quoting January 22, 2027 for delivery of the 256GB iPhone Duo in the U.S. and January 25, 2027 in the U.K. Estimates can change and depend on the configuration and delivery location.

Apple confirmed that its stores will have limited iPhone Duo stock for walk-in customers when sales begin on October 23. That offers another possibility for buyers facing long online delivery waits, but availability is not guaranteed and will vary by store.

If Apple’s delivery estimate is too far away, iPhone stock-checking services may help you locate another option. Apple Inventory Check monitors Apple Store availability, while TrackaLacker covers selected online retailers, including Best Buy and Walmart. Some notification features require registration or payment.

Apple described preorder demand as “nothing short of extraordinary” and said it was working to get devices to customers as quickly as possible.

Supply constraints may also contribute to the backlog. A late-September report claimed that Apple and its manufacturing partners were experiencing low production yields. Long delivery waits therefore reflect the balance between demand and available supply, rather than revealing how many phones Apple has sold.

iPhone Duo design: What does it look like?

Apple

The iPhone Duo uses a book-style folding design. Closed, it is unusually short and wide for an iPhone, measuring 84.1mm wide, 117.8mm tall and 11.3mm thick. Open it and the width expands to 164.6mm, while thickness reduces to just 5.2mm, making it Apple’s thinnest iPhone when unfolded (taking that mantle from the iPhone Air). It weighs 254g.

The outer screen measures 5.4 inches, while the folding inner panel measures 7.6 inches. Both are Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz, Always-On display support and up to 3,000 nits outdoor peak brightness. The internal display also has a nano-texture surface designed to reduce reflections and make the crease less noticeable. The inner display also has a replaceable top cover layer. AppleCare+ lists replacement at $19, although it must be replaced by Apple rather than peeled off like a conventional screen protector. Apple has not yet published the price without AppleCare+.

The frame and hinge cover are made from Grade 5 titanium. Apple uses a mirror-polished finish on the enclosure and a micro-blasted finish on the 3D-printed hinge cover. Ceramic Shield protects the rear, while Ceramic Shield 2 protects the outer display. The phone retains an IP68 rating despite its folding construction.

Apple

There are just two colors: Star White and Night Sky, essentially confirming the pre-event reports of silver/white and a very dark blue. For more information read about the iPhone Duo colors.

Action button and Camera Control

There is Camera Control, giving access to exposure, depth, zoom, cameras, styles and tone. It can also launch the new Siri Camera mode.

However, Apple’s Duo doesn’t feature an Action button. The regular iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max retain both the Action button and Camera Control, so this is one hardware-control compromise of the folding model.

Accessories

Apple is also launching two dedicated accessories for the foldable:

  • The iPhone Duo Case at $79/£79
  • The Duo Folio with Kickstand at $129/£129

Both became available to order on October 16. And there are plenty more of the best cases for iPhone Duo in our test reviews.

Face ID, Touch ID and the notch

Perhaps the most surprising difference between the iPhone Duo and Apple’s other flagship iPhones is that there is no Face ID.

Instead, Apple has brought back Touch ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button. It works whether the Duo is folded or unfolded, and Apple Watch can also be used to unlock the device. This confirms one of the most persistent pre-launch rumors.

The internal display therefore does not need the TrueDepth sensors used for Face ID. Its FaceTime camera sits beneath the display and disappears when it isn’t being used, giving the inner screen a largely uninterrupted surface.

The inner camera itself is hidden below the display rather than sitting permanently in a visible camera cutout. And yet, despite this and the absence of Face ID, there is still support for Dynamic Island.

Future Duo models could restore Face ID. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple has tested iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with an under-display Face ID sensor and camera on the outer screen. However, he suggests the technology could arrive with either the second or third generation, so its inclusion in the next model remains uncertain.

iPhone Duo cameras: What cameras does it have?

Apple

The Duo has a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system, comprising:

The Duo does not have variable aperture. Variable aperture is exclusive to the 48MP Fusion Main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

The biggest camera features for iPhone Duo

Duo Preview

The outer screen can show a live preview while somebody else is being photographed, allowing the subject to adjust their pose and framing.

Smart Take and Kid Cue

Smart Take detects when everybody is ready and automatically captures the shot. Kid Cue uses animations on the outer screen to encourage children to look towards the camera.

Two-screen shooting

The folding design supports unusual shooting configurations, including using the main cameras for selfies or group photos while seeing the composition on the other screen. Duo FaceTime can also put nearby participants onto the outer display.

Other notable camera features include 48MP macro photography, a 2x optical-quality crop from the Main camera, an under-display inner FaceTime camera, Dual Capture for simultaneous front-and-rear video, and 4K Dolby Vision recording at up to 120fps.

Rear cameras

The 48MP Fusion Main has an f/1.6 aperture, sensor-shift stabilization and can shoot 24MP or 48MP images. It also provides a 12MP, 2x optical-quality crop equivalent to a 52mm lens.

The 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide has a 13mm-equivalent lens, f/2.2 aperture and 120-degree field of view. It also supports 48MP macro photography and is the same Ultra Wide camera used by the iPhone 18 Pro family.

That means the Duo does not match the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max camera system. Those phones add a dedicated 48MP Fusion Telephoto and variable aperture on the Main camera, making the Pro models much more flexible for photography despite costing substantially less.

Pre-event reports were divided between a Main + Telephoto and Main + Ultra Wide arrangement. Apple ultimately chose Main + Ultra Wide, confirming the earlier reports that a dedicated telephoto could be sacrificed to save space.

Front cameras

On the outside is a 12MP Center Stage camera with an f/2.2 aperture. It supports Center Stage, automatic portrait/landscape framing, Dual Capture, Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5 and 4K Dolby Vision video at up to 60fps.

Inside is an under-display FaceTime camera with an f/1.8 aperture. Apple does not specify its megapixel resolution. It supports Center Stage for video calls and records at up to 1080p/60fps. Its major advantage is visual rather than photographic: the camera effectively disappears beneath the display when it isn’t being used.

iPhone Duo video features

The Main camera records 4K Dolby Vision at 24, 25, 30, 60, 100 or 120fps, with 4K/120fps also available for slo-mo. Cinematic mode reaches 4K/60fps and Action mode up to 2.8K/60fps. Dual Capture can record at up to 4K/30fps.

Apple’s specifications also do not list ProRes or Apple Log recording for the Duo. Those remain more Pro-oriented capabilities rather than part of Apple’s foldable camera proposition.

The Duo does support Spatial Audio recording, Audio Mix, Dolby Vision HDR and Apple’s computational photography features including Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5, Photographic Styles 3, smart focus tracking and Apple Intelligence-powered editing.

Apple does not list conventional Spatial Video capture in the Duo specifications.

iPhone Duo processor: What processor does it use?

Apple

The iPhone Duo uses the A20 Pro, the same processor as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, a major step forward in transistor density and efficiency. Apple combines it with a new chip packaging design inspired by its M-series Mac processors. The package connects the A20 Pro directly to a custom vapor chamber to transfer heat away from the processor more effectively.

The A20 Pro includes:

  • 6-core CPU: two super cores and four efficiency cores
  • 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators
  • Dual 16-core Neural Engine
  • Hardware-accelerated ray tracing
  • A dedicated display engine capable of operating both Duo displays

Compared with the A19 Pro, Apple says the CPU is up to 20 percent faster, while the GPU is up to 40 percent faster and more power-efficient. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers twice the compute power, while unified-memory bandwidth rises by 50 percent.

Apple also claims that the complete thermal system gives the Duo up to 35 percent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro. That sustained-performance figure is particularly important for a folding device because prolonged gaming, multitasking and AI workloads generate considerably more heat than short benchmark bursts.

iPhone Duo RAM: How much memory does it have?

Apple has not disclosed how much RAM is inside the iPhone Duo.

Before launch, supply-chain reports consistently pointed to 12GB of RAM, which would make sense given the demands of running two displays, simultaneous applications, Siri AI and larger on-device AI models.

Apple does reveal that A20 Pro has 50 percent more unified-memory bandwidth than A19 Pro, which should help the Duo move data more quickly between the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine.

Extra memory is particularly useful on the Duo because iOS 27.1 can display multiple apps simultaneously and because Apple Intelligence and Siri AI increasingly run generative models locally rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.

iPhone Duo connectivity

Apple

Apple has put a significant amount of its own communications silicon into the iPhone Duo.

It uses Apple’s new C2 cellular modem, replacing Qualcomm silicon. Apple says C2 introduces AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability and supports mmWave 5G in the U.S.

The N1 wireless networking chip provides:

  • Wi-Fi 7 with 2×2 MIMO
  • Bluetooth 6
  • Thread networking

The USB-C port also supports USB 3 data transfers at up to 10Gbps and DisplayPort video output.

The Duo also has Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, NFC and precision dual-frequency GPS.

It is eSIM-only worldwide, something that had been widely rumored before launch. Eliminating the SIM tray gives Apple additional internal space for its batteries.

iPhone Handoff – a feature introduced with iOS 27 – makes it easier to use an iPhone Duo alongside another iPhone without needing separate phone numbers. Both devices share your number, with calls, voicemail, messages and Find My location following whichever iPhone you unlock. Only one phone is active at a time. You could use the Duo’s folding display for work, then switch to an iPhone Pro when you want its telephoto camera. Both phones need iOS 27, eSIM support and the same Apple Account, with Messages in iCloud enabled. Your carrier must specifically support iPhone Handoff, and your plan may require an additional monthly fee for access. T-Mobile already offers iPhone Handoff for $5 a month; Verizon and EE (in the U.K.) plan support. Fees may apply.

Satellite capabilities include:

  • Emergency SOS via satellite
  • Roadside Assistance via satellite
  • Find My via satellite
  • Messages via satellite

Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s available?

Instead of one battery spanning the body, the iPhone Duo contains two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, with one high-energy battery fitted into each half of the device. Apple’s energy-balancing algorithms make them operate as a single battery system.

Apple rates battery life at:

  • Up to 24 hours of typical use
  • Up to 44 hours video playback using the outer display
  • Up to 31 hours using the inner display
  • Up to 37 hours streamed video on the outer screen
  • Up to 26 hours streamed video on the inner display

Early reviewers reported different battery experiences. CNET found the Duo comfortably lasted through a busy day, while The Verge questioned whether it could manage a full day of heavy use. These observations reflect different usage patterns and testing methods, so they should not be treated as directly comparable results or replacements for Apple’s playback ratings above.

Apple has not disclosed the batteries’ combined capacity in mAh. The pre-launch rumor of approximately 5,000-5,500mAh therefore remains unconfirmed.

Apple says the iPhone Duo can reach 50 percent charge in around 20 minutes using a USB-C charging cable and a 60W-capable power adapter or higher.

MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging are supported at up to 25W. Apple’s claimed 50 percent charge in around 30 minutes requires a MagSafe charger paired with a 35W-or-higher power adapter.

In both the U.S. and U.K., the box includes the iPhone Duo and a 1-meter USB-C charging cable, but no power adapter. The MagSafe charger is also sold separately, so factor these accessories into your budget if you don’t already own suitable equipment.

iPhone Duo price: How much does it cost?

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the U.S. and £1,999 in the U.K. for 256GB.

Prices are:

The 256GB starting capacity means Apple has not created an unusually low-storage entry model simply to make the headline price look lower.

iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro pricing

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. That makes the Duo approximately $700/£700 more expensive than the Pro Max at entry level.

That premium buys the folding display, precision hinge, titanium structure, second screen and more complex dual-battery design rather than superior cameras: in several areas the iPhone 18 Pro models are actually better equipped.

Reports before the launch suggested the Duo could cost anywhere from around $1,999 to $2,399 at entry level, largely because of the folding OLED display, hinge mechanism, titanium components and other expensive parts. Apple ultimately landed at the very bottom of those predictions.

iPhone Duo software: Multitasking and Apple Pencil support

The iPhone Duo’s larger inner display enables Split View, letting you use two apps side by side. For example, you could keep Safari open while taking notes, or check your calendar alongside a conversation in Messages. Supported apps can also open two windows of their own: Safari can display two webpages side by side for comparison shopping. You can save pairs of apps to return to later.

Early reviews suggest that third-party apps do not yet make good use of the larger display. Tom’s Guide and Wired encountered apps with black bars around them, while Tom’s Guide also reported poorly fitting game layouts.

App support is improving, however. Apple has highlighted that Netflix, Fantastical, MLB and Asphalt Legends will be among the apps optimized for launch, and says compatible apps carry a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their App Store product pages. Other updates are still coming: Microsoft Word and Outlook’s Duo-specific layouts are due in the coming weeks, while Zenless Zone Zero’s update is scheduled for November.

StandBy also works differently on the Duo. Set the phone down and it can display a clock, photos or widgets on either screen without being connected to a charger. New Calendar and Weather faces join the existing options.

Apple Pencil support is coming later in 2026. Apple has announced compatibility with the Apple Pencil (USB-C), allowing users to write, sketch and mark up documents on either display.

What do the first iPhone Duo reviews say?

The first independent reviews praise the Duo’s hinge, display and overall hardware design, while highlighting uneven app optimization and differing battery experiences. Reviewers generally enjoyed the folding experience, but their findings reinforce the importance of checking whether it suits your everyday needs.

Should you buy the iPhone Duo?

The iPhone Duo is the iPhone to buy if you genuinely want a phone and small tablet in one device. Its 7.6-inch display, multitasking features, A20 Pro performance and clever fold-specific camera modes offer capabilities no other iPhone has. 

But at $1,999/£1,999 it is enormously expensive, and there are significant compromises: no Face ID, no dedicated telephoto camera, no variable aperture and no Action button. 

For photography, battery life and conventional everyday use, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is likely to be the better-value flagship. Buy the Duo because you want the folding experience, not because it is simply the “best” iPhone.

Apple describes the internal screen as its largest-ever iPhone display, with 50 percent more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, while the outer display provides more than 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest difference is obviously the folding design, but Apple has done more than simply add a hinge. The iPhone Duo ships with iOS 27.1, which adapts to different positions and orientations with fold-specific interface and multitasking features. These include Split View, hands-free FaceTime and video, StandBy without charging, and layouts that move seamlessly between the two screens. Apple Pencil USB-C support is also coming later in 2026.

iPhone Duo design: What does it look like?

Apple

The iPhone Duo uses a book-style folding design. Closed, it is unusually short and wide for an iPhone, measuring 84.1mm wide, 117.8mm tall and 11.3mm thick. Open it and the width expands to 164.6mm, while thickness reduces to just 5.2mm, making it Apple’s thinnest iPhone when unfolded (taking that mantle from the iPhone Air). It weighs 254g.

The outer screen measures 5.4 inches, while the folding inner panel measures 7.6 inches. Both are Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz, Always-On display support and up to 3,000 nits outdoor peak brightness. The internal display also has a nano-texture surface designed to reduce reflections and make the crease less noticeable. The inner display also has a replaceable top cover layer. AppleCare+ lists replacement at $19, although it must be replaced by Apple rather than peeled off like a conventional screen protector. Apple has not yet published the price without AppleCare+.

The frame and hinge cover are made from Grade 5 titanium. Apple uses a mirror-polished finish on the enclosure and a micro-blasted finish on the 3D-printed hinge cover. Ceramic Shield protects the rear, while Ceramic Shield 2 protects the outer display. The phone retains an IP68 rating despite its folding construction.

Apple

There are just two colors: Star White and Night Sky, essentially confirming the pre-event reports of silver/white and a very dark blue. For more information read about the iPhone Duo colors.

Action button and Camera Control

There is Camera Control, giving access to exposure, depth, zoom, cameras, styles and tone. It can also launch the new Siri Camera mode.

However, Apple’s Duo doesn’t feature an Action button. The regular iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max retain both the Action button and Camera Control, so this is one hardware-control compromise of the folding model.

Accessories

Apple is also launching two dedicated accessories for the foldable:

  • The iPhone Duo Case at $79/£79
  • The Duo Folio with Kickstand at $129/£129

Both became available to order on October 16. And there are plenty more of the best cases for iPhone Duo in our test reviews.

Face ID, Touch ID and the notch

Perhaps the most surprising difference between the iPhone Duo and Apple’s other flagship iPhones is that there is no Face ID.

Instead, Apple has brought back Touch ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button. It works whether the Duo is folded or unfolded, and Apple Watch can also be used to unlock the device. This confirms one of the most persistent pre-launch rumors.

The internal display therefore does not need the TrueDepth sensors used for Face ID. Its FaceTime camera sits beneath the display and disappears when it isn’t being used, giving the inner screen a largely uninterrupted surface.

The inner camera itself is hidden below the display rather than sitting permanently in a visible camera cutout. And yet, despite this and the absence of Face ID, there is still support for Dynamic Island.

Future Duo models could restore Face ID. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple has tested iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with an under-display Face ID sensor and camera on the outer screen. However, he suggests the technology could arrive with either the second or third generation, so its inclusion in the next model remains uncertain.

The Duo has a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system, comprising:

The Duo does not have variable aperture. Variable aperture is exclusive to the 48MP Fusion Main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

The biggest camera features for iPhone Duo

Duo Preview

The outer screen can show a live preview while somebody else is being photographed, allowing the subject to adjust their pose and framing.

Smart Take and Kid Cue

Smart Take detects when everybody is ready and automatically captures the shot. Kid Cue uses animations on the outer screen to encourage children to look towards the camera.

Two-screen shooting

The folding design supports unusual shooting configurations, including using the main cameras for selfies or group photos while seeing the composition on the other screen. Duo FaceTime can also put nearby participants onto the outer display.

Other notable camera features include 48MP macro photography, a 2x optical-quality crop from the Main camera, an under-display inner FaceTime camera, Dual Capture for simultaneous front-and-rear video, and 4K Dolby Vision recording at up to 120fps.

Rear cameras

The 48MP Fusion Main has an f/1.6 aperture, sensor-shift stabilization and can shoot 24MP or 48MP images. It also provides a 12MP, 2x optical-quality crop equivalent to a 52mm lens.

The 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide has a 13mm-equivalent lens, f/2.2 aperture and 120-degree field of view. It also supports 48MP macro photography and is the same Ultra Wide camera used by the iPhone 18 Pro family.

That means the Duo does not match the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max camera system. Those phones add a dedicated 48MP Fusion Telephoto and variable aperture on the Main camera, making the Pro models much more flexible for photography despite costing substantially less.

Pre-event reports were divided between a Main + Telephoto and Main + Ultra Wide arrangement. Apple ultimately chose Main + Ultra Wide, confirming the earlier reports that a dedicated telephoto could be sacrificed to save space.

Front cameras

On the outside is a 12MP Center Stage camera with an f/2.2 aperture. It supports Center Stage, automatic portrait/landscape framing, Dual Capture, Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5 and 4K Dolby Vision video at up to 60fps.

The Main camera records 4K Dolby Vision at 24, 25, 30, 60, 100 or 120fps, with 4K/120fps also available for slo-mo. Cinematic mode reaches 4K/60fps and Action mode up to 2.8K/60fps. Dual Capture can record at up to 4K/30fps.

Apple does not list conventional Spatial Video capture in the Duo specifications.

iPhone Duo processor: What processor does it use?

Apple

The iPhone Duo uses the A20 Pro, the same processor as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, a major step forward in transistor density and efficiency. Apple combines it with a new chip packaging design inspired by its M-series Mac processors. The package connects the A20 Pro directly to a custom vapor chamber to transfer heat away from the processor more effectively.

The A20 Pro includes:

  • 6-core CPU: two super cores and four efficiency cores
  • 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators
  • Dual 16-core Neural Engine
  • Hardware-accelerated ray tracing
  • A dedicated display engine capable of operating both Duo displays

Compared with the A19 Pro, Apple says the CPU is up to 20 percent faster, while the GPU is up to 40 percent faster and more power-efficient. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers twice the compute power, while unified-memory bandwidth rises by 50 percent.

Apple also claims that the complete thermal system gives the Duo up to 35 percent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro. That sustained-performance figure is particularly important for a folding device because prolonged gaming, multitasking and AI workloads generate considerably more heat than short benchmark bursts.

iPhone Duo RAM: How much memory does it have?

Apple has not disclosed how much RAM is inside the iPhone Duo.

Before launch, supply-chain reports consistently pointed to 12GB of RAM, which would make sense given the demands of running two displays, simultaneous applications, Siri AI and larger on-device AI models.

Apple does reveal that A20 Pro has 50 percent more unified-memory bandwidth than A19 Pro, which should help the Duo move data more quickly between the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine.

Extra memory is particularly useful on the Duo because iOS 27.1 can display multiple apps simultaneously and because Apple Intelligence and Siri AI increasingly run generative models locally rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.

iPhone Duo connectivity

Apple

Apple has put a significant amount of its own communications silicon into the iPhone Duo.

It uses Apple’s new C2 cellular modem, replacing Qualcomm silicon. Apple says C2 introduces AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability and supports mmWave 5G in the U.S.

The N1 wireless networking chip provides:

  • Wi-Fi 7 with 2×2 MIMO
  • Bluetooth 6
  • Thread networking

The USB-C port also supports USB 3 data transfers at up to 10Gbps and DisplayPort video output.

The Duo also has Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, NFC and precision dual-frequency GPS.

It is eSIM-only worldwide, something that had been widely rumored before launch. Eliminating the SIM tray gives Apple additional internal space for its batteries.

iPhone Handoff – a feature introduced with iOS 27 – makes it easier to use an iPhone Duo alongside another iPhone without needing separate phone numbers. Both devices share your number, with calls, voicemail, messages and Find My location following whichever iPhone you unlock. Only one phone is active at a time. You could use the Duo’s folding display for work, then switch to an iPhone Pro when you want its telephoto camera. Both phones need iOS 27, eSIM support and the same Apple Account, with Messages in iCloud enabled. Your carrier must specifically support iPhone Handoff, and your plan may require an additional monthly fee for access. T-Mobile already offers iPhone Handoff for $5 a month; Verizon and EE (in the U.K.) plan support. Fees may apply.

Satellite capabilities include:

  • Emergency SOS via satellite
  • Roadside Assistance via satellite
  • Find My via satellite
  • Messages via satellite

Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s available?

Instead of one battery spanning the body, the iPhone Duo contains two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, with one high-energy battery fitted into each half of the device. Apple’s energy-balancing algorithms make them operate as a single battery system.

Apple rates battery life at:

  • Up to 24 hours of typical use
  • Up to 44 hours video playback using the outer display
  • Up to 31 hours using the inner display
  • Up to 37 hours streamed video on the outer screen
  • Up to 26 hours streamed video on the inner display

Early reviewers reported different battery experiences. CNET found the Duo comfortably lasted through a busy day, while The Verge questioned whether it could manage a full day of heavy use. These observations reflect different usage patterns and testing methods, so they should not be treated as directly comparable results or replacements for Apple’s playback ratings above.

Apple has not disclosed the batteries’ combined capacity in mAh. The pre-launch rumor of approximately 5,000-5,500mAh therefore remains unconfirmed.

Apple says the iPhone Duo can reach 50 percent charge in around 20 minutes using a USB-C charging cable and a 60W-capable power adapter or higher.

MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging are supported at up to 25W. Apple’s claimed 50 percent charge in around 30 minutes requires a MagSafe charger paired with a 35W-or-higher power adapter.

In both the U.S. and U.K., the box includes the iPhone Duo and a 1-meter USB-C charging cable, but no power adapter. The MagSafe charger is also sold separately, so factor these accessories into your budget if you don’t already own suitable equipment.

iPhone Duo price: How much does it cost?

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the U.S. and £1,999 in the U.K. for 256GB.

Prices are:

The 256GB starting capacity means Apple has not created an unusually low-storage entry model simply to make the headline price look lower.

iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro pricing

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. That makes the Duo approximately $700/£700 more expensive than the Pro Max at entry level.

That premium buys the folding display, precision hinge, titanium structure, second screen and more complex dual-battery design rather than superior cameras: in several areas the iPhone 18 Pro models are actually better equipped.

Reports before the launch suggested the Duo could cost anywhere from around $1,999 to $2,399 at entry level, largely because of the folding OLED display, hinge mechanism, titanium components and other expensive parts. Apple ultimately landed at the very bottom of those predictions.

iPhone Duo software: Multitasking and Apple Pencil support

The iPhone Duo’s larger inner display enables Split View, letting you use two apps side by side. For example, you could keep Safari open while taking notes, or check your calendar alongside a conversation in Messages. Supported apps can also open two windows of their own: Safari can display two webpages side by side for comparison shopping. You can save pairs of apps to return to later.

Early reviews suggest that third-party apps do not yet make good use of the larger display. Tom’s Guide and Wired encountered apps with black bars around them, while Tom’s Guide also reported poorly fitting game layouts.

App support is improving, however. Apple has highlighted that Netflix, Fantastical, MLB and Asphalt Legends will be among the apps optimized for launch, and says compatible apps carry a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their App Store product pages. Other updates are still coming: Microsoft Word and Outlook’s Duo-specific layouts are due in the coming weeks, while Zenless Zone Zero’s update is scheduled for November.

StandBy also works differently on the Duo. Set the phone down and it can display a clock, photos or widgets on either screen without being connected to a charger. New Calendar and Weather faces join the existing options.

Apple Pencil support is coming later in 2026. Apple has announced compatibility with the Apple Pencil (USB-C), allowing users to write, sketch and mark up documents on either display.

What do the first iPhone Duo reviews say?

The first independent reviews praise the Duo’s hinge, display and overall hardware design, while highlighting uneven app optimization and differing battery experiences. Reviewers generally enjoyed the folding experience, but their findings reinforce the importance of checking whether it suits your everyday needs.

Should you buy the iPhone Duo?

The iPhone Duo is the iPhone to buy if you genuinely want a phone and small tablet in one device. Its 7.6-inch display, multitasking features, A20 Pro performance and clever fold-specific camera modes offer capabilities no other iPhone has. 

But at $1,999/£1,999 it is enormously expensive, and there are significant compromises: no Face ID, no dedicated telephoto camera, no variable aperture and no Action button. 

For photography, battery life and conventional everyday use, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is likely to be the better-value flagship. Buy the Duo because you want the folding experience, not because it is simply the “best” iPhone.

We see them all the time when there’s a new game console launch, or some hard-to-find sneakers, or during that brief Stanley Cup craze. But it has been a while since an iPhone launch has needed one. Usually. But the iPhone Duo is different. Notoriously difficult to manufacture and thus in limited supply, preorders at launch are now stretching into late January of 2027. That’s a three-month wait if you order now. You might do better buying an iPhone Duo from your carrier. Or trying to grab one of the modest retail resupplies that will trickle out over the coming weeks. That’s where stock-checking sites come in.

The early reviews of the iPhone Duo posted on Wednesday, and one common complaint is how some third-party apps look on the device. The iPhone Duo has new dimensions, and that often results in a suboptimal user experience. One reviewer went so far as to call them “horrible.”

In these situations, apps are not yet optimized for the iPhone Duo. Apps that are made for iPhone Duo can provide quite rewarding experiences, as Apple points out in an article it released to the media on Thursday. “From watching popular shows and content on the expansive inner display to multitasking across windows or playing console-quality games, developers around the world are reimagining what their apps can do,” said Apple VP Susan Prescott in the press release.

Apple

Video apps are taking advantage of the bigger folding display by providing modes that work when the Duo is propped open in an L shape; the top display shows the video while the bottom can display video controls and other items, as shown on the Netflix app. The Paramount+ app does a similar thing, but the bottom display can show info on the show being watched.

Sports fans can have a great time watching the game in apps made for iPhone Duo. The screen can be split so that live game coverage is streamed on one half, while the other provides a vast array of statistics, scores, and other data, as with the MLB app, which will be available on day one, in time for the World Series.

Apple

Productivity apps such as Bear, Fantastical, Notewise, Salesforce, Slack, Things, and Zoom take advantage of the larger inner display, and Microsoft Word and Outlook take advantage of the Duo’s Split View. Creative apps such as Detail, Instagram Edits, and VLLO provide an enhanced UI for video editing. Apple says apps that have been optimized will have a clear “Made for iPhone Duo” badge in the App Store.

Of course, games provide a better experience on the Duo’s big screen. Game such as Asphalt Legends, Retrocade, Sneaky Sasquatch, Ungodly, Zenless Zone Zero have been optimized for the new phone. “The large inner display and the sustained performance of A20 Pro let us put more of the track and every detail of our cars in front of users, so races look and feel incredible wherever they play,” said Raúl Orrego del Río, of Gameloft, creator of Asphalt Legends.

While Apple’s press release lists several more apps optimized for iPhone Duo, there are still many more that are not. It’s not a new situation; when Apple introduced the iPad, iPhone 5, and iPhone X, several developers had their apps ready for the device launch, but a vast majority were not. Developers need some time to catch up, so if your favorite app looks odd on your iPhone Duo, be sure to check the App Store for updates. There could be one waiting for your Duo.

Apps that are made for iPhone Duo can provide quite rewarding experiences, as Apple points out in an article it released to the media on Thursday. “From watching popular shows and content on the expansive inner display to multitasking across windows or playing console-quality games, developers around the world are reimagining what their apps can do,” said Apple VP Susan Prescott in the press release.

Apple

Video apps are taking advantage of the bigger folding display by providing modes that work when the Duo is propped open in an L shape; the top display shows the video while the bottom can display video controls and other items, as shown on the Netflix app. The Paramount+ app does a similar thing, but the bottom display can show info on the show being watched.

Sports fans can have a great time watching the game in apps made for iPhone Duo. The screen can be split so that live game coverage is streamed on one half, while the other provides a vast array of statistics, scores, and other data, as with the MLB app, which will be available on day one, in time for the World Series.

Apple

Productivity apps such as Bear, Fantastical, Notewise, Salesforce, Slack, Things, and Zoom take advantage of the larger inner display, and Microsoft Word and Outlook take advantage of the Duo’s Split View. Creative apps such as Detail, Instagram Edits, and VLLO provide an enhanced UI for video editing. Apple says apps that have been optimized will have a clear “Made for iPhone Duo” badge in the App Store.

Of course, games provide a better experience on the Duo’s big screen. Game such as Asphalt Legends, Retrocade, Sneaky Sasquatch, Ungodly, Zenless Zone Zero have been optimized for the new phone. “The large inner display and the sustained performance of A20 Pro let us put more of the track and every detail of our cars in front of users, so races look and feel incredible wherever they play,” said Raúl Orrego del Río, of Gameloft, creator of Asphalt Legends.

While Apple’s press release lists several more apps optimized for iPhone Duo, there are still many more that are not. It’s not a new situation; when Apple introduced the iPad, iPhone 5, and iPhone X, several developers had their apps ready for the device launch, but a vast majority were not. Developers need some time to catch up, so if your favorite app looks odd on your iPhone Duo, be sure to check the App Store for updates. There could be one waiting for your Duo.

Macworld will be posting an in-depth review of the iPhone Duo soon. In the meantime, check out our guide to everything you need to know about the iPhone Duo.
